problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response states that the nth-term test runs one way only --- terms not approaching zero prove divergence, but terms approaching zero prove nothing. The harmonic series is the standard counterexample and it is the very series in front of the student. Full credit says the test was used in the direction it does not have.

problems.slot: the value at the left endpoint

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response says the ratio test settles only the open interval, because at an endpoint the ratio limit equals one and the test is silent there by construction. Each endpoint must be substituted back and tested separately; here the left endpoint gives the alternating harmonic series and belongs in the interval, while the right endpoint gives the harmonic series and does not.

traps.desc: used the last term included instead of the first term omitted

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response states the alternating series remainder bound in its exact form --- the error after N terms is at most the size of term number N plus one --- and points out that the student used term number N instead. Full credit says which index the bound reads and why it is the first OMITTED term that matters.

traps.desc: used one as the first term instead of the term at n equal to two

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response says the geometric formula divides the FIRST TERM ACTUALLY WRITTEN by one minus the ratio, and that the starting index changes that first term. Here the sum starts at two, so the first term is one sixteenth rather than one. Full credit states the rule in a way that survives any starting index.

Part (c): a correct response says a ratio limit of one means the ratio test reaches NO conclusion, so nothing at all had been established. Limit comparison against the harmonic series then gives a finite positive limit, and since the harmonic series diverges so does this one. Full credit states that the ratio test is guaranteed to return one for terms that are a ratio of polynomials.

traps.desc: read the radius off the shifted variable without factoring the two out

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response rewrites the shifted power so the coefficient on the variable is visible, giving a centre of three and a radius of one half, then tests both endpoints and reports a half-open interval. Full credit names both faults in the student work --- the unfactored coefficient and the missing endpoint tests.

traps.desc: subtracted one from the exponent instead of adding one when antidifferentiating

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response names both faults. First, antidifferentiating a power ADDS one to the exponent and divides by the new exponent, so the antiderivative is minus two over the square root of x. Second, the integral test decides convergence but its value is not the sum of the series --- the sum lies between the integral and the integral plus the first term. Full credit gives both.
